As of December 31, 2023, Boeing’s 10-K lists these shares of employees represented:

- **21%** — International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (**IAM**)
- **10%** — Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (**SPEEA**)
- **1%** — United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (**UAW**)

The filing also says approximately **57,000 employees** were union members. The three listed percentages total **32%**; a separate risk-factor summary describes union representation as **33%** of the workforce.

The filing identifies these 2025 developments in its legal-proceedings disclosures and related risk discussion:

| Date | Development |
|---|---|
| **April 23, 2025** | The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** in its DMA investigation into App Store steering and ordered Apple to remove certain restrictions on developers. The Commission also issued **preliminary findings** in a separate DMA investigation concerning Apple’s contractual requirements for developers. Apple appealed the fine and said it believed it complied with the DMA. |
| **April 30, 2025** | In the Epic Games case, the California District Court found Apple had violated the 2021 injunction. It barred Apple from imposing fees on certain purchases outside apps or restricting how developers direct users to those purchases, denied Apple’s request to narrow or vacate the injunction, and referred the matter for consideration of possible criminal-contempt proceedings. Apple appealed. |
| **September 2, 2025** | In the U.S. antitrust case against **Google**, a court ordered remedies after finding Google had violated antitrust laws in 2024. The filing says the order could change through further proceedings and appeals; a reversal could lead to remedies affecting Google’s commercial search-distribution arrangements with Apple. |
| **October 2025** | The Ninth Circuit heard expedited oral arguments in Apple’s appeal of the Epic Games ruling. |

*Source: Apple 2025 Form 10-K, pp. 14 and 18.*

The filing gives two different timelines:

| Item | What the filing says | What it refers to |
|---|---|---|
| **2025 IAM District 837 strike** | Approximately **3,200 employees**; **101 days**; began **August 4, 2025**, and ended when employees ratified a new contract on **November 13, 2025**. | The employees represented at Boeing’s **St. Louis-area sites** and the duration of the work stoppage. The filing says it disrupted St. Louis operations and affected programs including F/A-18, F-15, T-7A, MQ-25 and Weapons. |
| **Current District 837 agreement** | The agreement is listed for **Missouri**, with an expiration in **July 2030**. | The scheduled expiration of Boeing’s collective bargaining agreement with IAM District 837—not the duration of the 2025 strike. The filing gives only the month and year, not an exact expiration day or an explicit contract term. |

The strike and agreement details appear in the filing’s Human Capital discussion and MD&A overview. The November 13 date is the **ratification date that ended the stoppage**; the filing does not identify it as the agreement’s effective date.

Apple said foreign-currency weakness was a headwind to:

- **Net sales in Greater China**, where the weaker **renminbi** adversely affected sales year over year.
- **Net sales in Japan**, where the weaker **yen** had an unfavorable impact.
- **Net sales in Rest of Asia Pacific**, where weaker foreign currencies had a net unfavorable impact.
- **Products gross margin and Products gross-margin percentage**: both increased in 2024, but currency weakness partly offset the increases.

These statements appear in the fiscal 2024 Form 10-K’s segment and gross-margin discussion (pp. 22, 24). Apple did not attribute the same currency headwind to every reported result.

Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K reports:

- **Net sales by distribution channel:** Direct channels accounted for **40%** and indirect channels **60%** of fiscal 2025 total net sales.
- **Trade receivables at September 27, 2025:** One customer accounted for **12%** of total trade receivables; third-party cellular network carriers accounted for **34%**.
- **Vendor non-trade receivables at September 27, 2025:** Two vendors accounted for **46%** and **23%**, respectively, of total vendor non-trade receivables.

The customer and vendor disclosures also mention a **10%** figure as the threshold for identifying which customers or vendors are specifically disclosed; it is not an additional share to report. (Form 10-K pp. 2, 39.)

The filing gives four percentages:

- **46%** — Boeing’s **total 2025 revenue** came from non-U.S. customers, including Foreign Military Sales through the U.S. government.
- **60%** — **Commercial Airplanes revenue from customer contracts** came from non-U.S. customers.
- **Approximately 85%** — **Commercial Airplanes’ total backlog**, by dollar value, was with non-U.S. airlines.
- **26%** — **Defense, Space & Security backlog** was attributable to non-U.S. customers.

The revenue figures are on page 12; the backlog figures are on pages 35 and 40 of the filing.

Boeing’s 2022 Form 10-K reports these shares of segment revenue as recognized on fixed-price contracts:

- **Commercial Airplanes (BCA): 100%**
- **Defense, Space & Security (BDS): 60%**
- **Global Services (BGS): 88%**

These figures appear in Note 22, “Segment and Revenue Information” (filing pages 111–112).

Excluding the **6.00% rate** and the **$1,000-per-share liquidation preference**, the 10-K gives these dividend amounts:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$12.50 per preferred share** | The dividend per share declared in December 2024 for holders of record January 1, 2025. |
| **$72 million** | The total dividend declared in December 2024; Boeing says it was paid in cash on January 15, 2025. |
| **$58 million** | Preferred dividends accumulated during 2024, deducted in calculating net loss attributable to common shareholders. |
| **Up to $345 million per year** | Boeing’s estimate of the cash it might need for preferred dividends annually through the October 15, 2027 mandatory conversion date. |

The **$72 million** declaration and the **$58 million** accumulated during 2024 describe different things: the first was payable in January 2025, while the second was the amount accumulated during the 2024 reporting period. The filing presents the figures in millions except for the per-share amount. (Form 10-K pp. 17, 54, 106.)

The filing describes these effects:

- **Products, services, and support were blocked from reaching Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine** by the sanctions and export controls imposed in response to the war.
- **NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia and closed its Russian business operations** during fiscal 2023. Direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2022 had been immaterial.
- **The war affected end-customer sales in EMEA.**
- **Revenue from partners selling into Russia may have been negatively affected** by the war.

These are the effects the filing says had occurred or may have occurred; I have excluded consequences it describes only as future risks. *(Form 10-K, pp. 28, 37)*

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2026 Form 10-K gives these goodwill amounts, in millions unless noted:

- **$20.8 billion at January 25, 2026** — total goodwill, allocated as **$20.5 billion to Compute & Networking** and **$370 million to Graphics**.
- **$15.6 billion added during fiscal 2026** — the increase in goodwill for the year; it was allocated to **Compute & Networking**.
- **$14.4 billion recorded for the Groq technology license** — goodwill primarily attributable to the workforce and future development of the licensed technology. NVIDIA recorded it in the **Compute & Networking reporting unit** and said it was tax deductible.

The $14.4 billion Groq-related amount is part of the fiscal-year goodwill activity, not an additional balance to add to the year-end total. (Form 10-K, pp. 61, 63.)

The filing identifies two operating businesses with 2024 affiliate-borrowing figures:

| Business | Affiliate borrowing disclosed for 2024 |
|---|---|
| **Clayton Homes** | Borrowings from Berkshire finance affiliates **increased $6.6 billion**, reaching **$24.3 billion at year-end**. |
| **Pilot Travel Centers** | Borrowed **$5.7 billion** from Berkshire insurance subsidiaries in March and repaid **$1.0 billion** during the year. That implies about **$4.7 billion** remained outstanding, though the filing does not state that year-end affiliate balance directly. |

Sources: Form 10-K, MD&A pages K-48 and K-53; Note 19, page K-99.

For fiscal 2024, NVIDIA disclosed:

- **$774 million** charged to cost of revenue as an inventory provision—write-downs for excess or obsolete inventory.
- **Approximately $1.4 billion** charged to cost of revenue for inventory purchase obligations exceeding current demand projections, including supplier charges and penalties for cancellations and underutilization.
- **$2.2 billion total** in provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations, as reported in the MD&A. The two component amounts above are rounded disclosures.
- **$540 million released** from provisions when previously reserved inventory was sold or excess inventory purchase obligations were settled. NVIDIA gave this as a combined release; it did not separately quantify the two sources.

The charges and release are described on pages 40, 68 and 70 of the filing.

The filing reports the following **PTC-specific balances at December 31, 2023**. Amounts shown in millions are from tables stated in millions; figures described as “approximately” are approximate.

| Balance | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Identifiable assets at year-end | **$21.404 billion** |
| Goodwill at year-end | **$6.605 billion** |
| Net carrying value of intangible assets | **Approximately $6.6 billion** |
| Notes payable and other borrowings | **$5.776 billion** |
| Portion of railroad, utilities and energy inventories attributable to PTC | **Approximately $1.7 billion** |
| Portion of railroad, utilities and energy receivables related to PTC | **Approximately $2.1 billion** |

The identifiable-assets and goodwill figures are listed separately in the year-end business-segment table (Note 26, p. K-114). The intangible-assets amount is identified as PTC-related in Note 13 (p. K-91); debt is listed for PTC and its subsidiaries in Note 19 (p. K-102); the inventory and receivables amounts are specified in Notes 9 and 8, respectively (p. K-89 and K-88).

I have excluded year flows, acquisition-date amounts, and balances shown only for combined businesses without a separately stated PTC portion.

Pfizer’s 2024 Form 10-K gives these Haleon ownership percentages:

- **32%** at **December 31, 2023**.
- **Approximately 23%** after Pfizer’s **March 2024** share sale.
- **Approximately 15%** after the **October 2024** sale, and **as of December 31, 2024**.

These figures appear in Note 3C, “Equity-Method Investments” (Form 10-K page 66).

The filing identifies **$1.008 billion in net fiscal 2025 gains** on equity securities, combining the amounts below. Amounts are in millions:

| Investment type | Amount | What it represents |
|---|---:|---|
| Publicly held | **+$163** | Net unrealized gains for fiscal 2025 on securities held at year-end. |
| Publicly held | **+$88** | Realized gains on securities sold—the difference between sale proceeds and their carrying value at the beginning of the period or, if later, their purchase date. |
| Non-marketable | **+$816** | Unrealized gains recorded as adjustments to the carrying value of these investments. |
| Non-marketable | **−$59** | Impairments and unrealized losses recorded as carrying-value adjustments. |

The non-marketable amounts net to **+$757 million**; the publicly held amounts net to **+$251 million**. Together, they net to **+$1.008 billion**. The filing says a **$565 million** unrealized gain from a private-company investment’s fourth-quarter secondary equity transaction is **included in** the $816 million—not an additional gain. (pp. 66, 68–69.)

This excludes the separate **cumulative** gross unrealized gains and cumulative gross unrealized losses and impairments on non-marketable securities still held at year-end.

The filing gives these Upjohn separation-cost figures:

- **“approximately $700 million”** — Pfizer’s expected total costs in connection with separating Upjohn. The filing says these include costs and expenses related to the separation of legal entities and transaction costs. **“approximately 75%”** of that total had been incurred from inception through December 31, 2021. (MD&A, p. 26)
- **“$434 million in 2020 and $83 million in 2019”** — separation-related costs Pfizer incurred in those respective years, included in discontinued operations. The filing says they primarily related to professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities in finance, tax, legal and information systems, as well as investment-banking fees. (Note 2, p. 65)

The filing gives separate counts for **Walmart U.S.** and **Walmart International**:

- **Walmart U.S.**: approximately **4,600 pickup locations** and **more than 3,500 same-day delivery locations**. These are described as part of Walmart U.S.’s omnichannel services. (p. 7)
- **Walmart International**: approximately **2,900 pickup locations** and **over 1,900 delivery locations**. The filing does not label that delivery-location count as “same-day.” (p. 9)

The 10-K reports these adoption effects, in millions:

| Amount | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **$587 decrease** | The Firm’s net decrease in the **allowance for credit losses** from adopting the TDR guidance on January 1, 2023, under the modified-retrospective method. In the allowance-for-loan-losses table, the decrease is allocated as **$489 for Consumer excluding credit card**, **$100 for Credit card**, and **$2 increase for Wholesale**—a net **$587 decrease**. |
| **$591 decrease** | The separately reported decrease in the **Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) segment’s allowance for loan losses**. The filing says it was driven by residential real estate and credit card. This is a segment-specific figure, not an additional Firm-wide reduction. |
| **$446 increase** | The increase in **retained earnings, after tax**, resulting from the adoption. |

The Firm-wide allowance decrease and retained-earnings increase are the adoption’s cumulative opening-balance effects; the $591 figure is the CCB segment disclosure. The filing describes the accounting change as moving most modified loans to troubled borrowers from an asset-specific to a non-DCF portfolio-based allowance approach, while retaining the asset-specific approach for collateral-dependent and nonaccrual risk-rated loans.

*Sources: 2023 Form 10-K, MD&A pp. 132 and 70; Note 1 p. 173; Note 13 pp. 256–258.*

The 10-K reports **two related figures** for fiscal 2025:

- **$3,468 million** — “Repayments of long-term debt” in the fiscal-year debt rollforward (MD&A, p. 44).
- Note 6 lists these **significant repayments of matured debt** (p. 69):
  - **$1,500 million** — April 22, 2024 maturity
  - **$990 million** — July 8, 2024 maturity
  - **$253 million** — July 18, 2024 maturity; the table gives the principal as **¥40,000 million**
  - **$630 million** — December 15, 2024 maturity  
  **Total repayment of matured debt: $3,373 million.**

The filing presents the $3,468 million as the rollforward repayment figure and $3,373 million as the total of the significant matured-debt repayments itemized in Note 6.

The 2021 Form 10-K identifies these projects:

- **Bacalhau Phase 1, Brazil** — funded in 2021; ExxonMobil also announced its final investment decision in June.
- **North Field Production Sustainment Integrated Drilling and Looping project, Qatar** — funded in 2021.
- **Jansz-Io Compression project, Australia** — funded in 2021.
- **Huizhou chemical complex, China** — ExxonMobil reached a final investment decision to proceed with the multi-billion-dollar project.

The report mentions Bacalhau in both the funded-project discussion and the final-investment-decision discussion. (Form 10-K pp. 16–18, 46, 53.)

The 10-K lists Huizhou’s annual capacity as:

- **1.6 million metric tons of ethylene**
- **1.7 million metric tons of polyethylene**
- **0.9 million metric tons of polypropylene**

These are separate product-capacity figures for the complex, not a combined total. The table shows ExxonMobil’s interest as **100%** and no refining capacity for Huizhou. (Form 10-K, p. 23.)

For the **receive fixed-rate, pay fixed-rate cross-currency swaps designated as cash flow hedges**, the filing gives these amounts:

- **$6,020 million** — the swaps’ **notional amount** as of January 31, 2026.
- **$920 million liability** — their **fair value**; the fair-value table shows it as **$(920) million**. The market-risk discussion rounds this to a **$0.9 billion liability**.
- **$0.7 billion** — the hypothetical change in swap value if the U.S. dollar weakened uniformly by 10% against the currencies underlying the swaps.
- **$0.1 billion** — the hypothetical change in swap value if interest rates underlying the swaps changed by 10% from January 31, 2026 market rates.

The last two are **sensitivities, not additional balances**. The swaps hedge currency exposure on forecast principal and interest payments for certain non-U.S.-denominated debt. (Form 10-K, pp. 47, 61, 69.)

The 10-K gives these quantified annual sensitivities:

| Change | Stated annual effect |
|---|---|
| **Brent crude price:** $1 per barrel | Approximately **$700 million after tax** on 2026 Upstream earnings, consolidated plus equity companies, excluding derivatives |
| **Henry Hub natural-gas price:** $0.10 per million Btu | Approximately **$90 million after tax** on 2026 Upstream earnings, consolidated plus equity companies, excluding derivatives |
| **TTF natural-gas price:** $0.10 per million Btu | Approximately **$20 million after tax** on 2026 Upstream earnings, consolidated plus equity companies, excluding derivatives |
| **Expected return on pension-plan assets:** a worldwide reduction of 0.5 percentage point | Approximately **$150 million higher annual pension expense before tax** |

For the market-price sensitivities, the report says the effects may be positive or negative depending on the direction of the price change and other factors. It also says a 100-basis-point change in interest rates affecting debt would not be material to earnings or cash flow, but gives no dollar amount. (Market Risks, p. 62; Pension Benefits, p. 67.)

Apple says quarter-to-quarter net sales can differ because:

- **Seasonality:** Sales have historically been higher in the first fiscal quarter, partly because of holiday demand.
- **Product and service introductions:** Launches can significantly affect net sales.
- **Dependence on one product:** A decline in demand for the product that accounts for a significant share of sales can materially affect quarterly sales.
- **Unexpected developments:** Lower-than-anticipated demand; problems with new launches; IT-system failures or network disruptions; or failures at logistics, component-supply, or manufacturing partners.

*Source: Apple FY2023 Form 10-K, p. 18 of the filing (printed page 15).*

The 2024 Form 10-K gives these measures of Pioneer’s scale or contribution:

- **Share of ExxonMobil:** Pioneer was a wholly owned subsidiary and represented **19% of ExxonMobil’s total assets** at year-end and **4% of its total revenues** for 2024. Pioneer was excluded from the internal-control assessment because it had been acquired during the year. (Management’s report on internal control, p. 73.)
- **2024 results:** From the acquisition date, **May 3, through December 31**, Pioneer contributed **$17.008 billion in sales and other operating revenues** and **$1.710 billion in net income attributable to ExxonMobil**. (Note 21, p. 119.)
- **Proved reserves:** The reserve discussion identifies **2.3 billion oil-equivalent barrels** of 2024 proved-reserve additions related to the Pioneer acquisition. This is an acquisition-related addition, not a separate year-end total for Pioneer’s reserves. (Supplemental oil and gas information, p. 125.)

The filing does not give a separate Pioneer-only year-end reserve total in those disclosures.

Berkshire said it recorded the charges after a **quantitative impairment reassessment in the second quarter of 2020**, focused especially on Precision Castparts (PCC). The initial effects of COVID-19 had been particularly severe for commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers. In evaluating the outlook, Berkshire considered airlines’ announcements about expected demand, employment levels and aircraft orders; manufacturers’ announced production cuts; and restructuring actions it had taken or might take.

Given those circumstances, Berkshire judged it prudent to **raise the discount rates and reduce its prior long-term cash-flow forecasts** used in the impairment review. The resulting pre-tax charges were $10.0 billion for goodwill and $638 million for indefinite-lived intangible assets; nearly all related to PCC, whose goodwill and intangible assets had largely been recorded when Berkshire acquired it in 2016. (2021 Form 10-K, p. 65.)

The filing identifies these fiscal 2024 improvements as benefiting from lapping fiscal 2023 items:

| Result | Lapped item named |
|---|---|
| **Gross profit rate**—the consolidated increase was driven primarily by Walmart U.S.; the U.S. segment’s rate also rose | Higher markdowns incurred in fiscal 2023 (described for Walmart U.S. as higher **net** markdowns). |
| **Sam’s Club gross profit rate** | Elevated markdowns in the prior year. |
| **Operating expenses as a percentage of net sales**, consolidated | $3.3 billion of opioid-related legal-settlement charges and $0.8 billion of charges for reorganizing and restructuring certain Walmart International businesses, both incurred in fiscal 2023. |
| **Walmart International operating expenses as a percentage of segment net sales** | Business reorganization and restructuring charges related to Flipkart and Massmart, incurred in fiscal 2023. |
| **Return on investment (ROI)** | Opioid-related legal-settlement charges and reorganization and restructuring expenses, all recorded in fiscal 2023. |

The filing also links increases in operating income or operating margin to the factors discussed above. I have not counted those as separate lapping results because it does not identify additional lapped items for them. (Form 10-K, pp. 38, 41–44)

The 10-K explicitly ties these figures to Flipkart or a Flipkart business:

| Amount or percentage | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$3.2 billion** | Cash Walmart received in fiscal 2022, **primarily from new equity funding for its majority-owned Flipkart subsidiary**. The funding reduced Walmart’s ownership from **approximately 83%** at January 31, 2021, to **approximately 75%**. (pp. 43, 64) |
| **Approximately 83% → approximately 75%** | Walmart’s ownership of Flipkart before and after that funding. (pp. 43, 64) |
| **$2.2 billion** | Of Walmart’s restricted cash at January 31, 2022, the amount accessible only through dividends or intercompany financing subject to Flipkart minority-shareholder approval; Walmart expected Flipkart to use it. (p. 42) |
| **$0.4 billion** | Fiscal 2020 impairment charges in Walmart International, consisting primarily of writing off the carrying value of Jabong.com, one of Flipkart’s two fashion trade names. (p. 71) |

I’ve excluded Walmart International’s broader segment figures and other company-wide totals that include Flipkart but aren’t identified as Flipkart-related in the passage.
Higher average deposits associated with First Republic, whose deposits were transferred from Consumer & Community Banking to Asset & Wealth Management in the fourth quarter of 2023.

The filing attributes PCC’s $853 million (11.6%) revenue decline in 2021 to the continuing effects of COVID-19. The pandemic sharply reduced commercial air travel and aircraft makers’ production. PCC’s lower aircraft-related sales reflected reduced build rates, airline order delays and cancellations, and industry-wide efforts to reduce inventories, including customer destocking at extraordinary rates. The filing also says delays in Boeing’s 737 MAX and 787 programs adversely affected PCC’s aerospace business during this period.

These effects were not confined to 2021: the filing says the pandemic harmed PCC’s aerospace business in both 2020 and 2021. (Form 10-K, pp. K-12 and K-49.)

The filing says these securities are investments in private companies with no readily determinable fair values. NVIDIA therefore uses the measurement alternative: it starts with cost, adjusts for impairment and observable transactions in similar investments of the same issuer, and may need to estimate value using unobservable inputs. Those inputs include volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and rights and obligations specific to the security. It also assesses impairment quarterly using qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee’s operating performance and market trends. These estimates and assessments require judgment. (Form 10-K, pp. 38, 66–67.)

Elevated consumer cash balances kept credit-card charge-offs lower and recoveries higher. Higher vehicle collateral values and elevated consumer cash balances reduced scored-auto charge-offs. Improved home prices and more reversals of prior write-downs due to prepayments in the low-rate environment increased residential real-estate recoveries.

Pfizer attributed the increase primarily to the 2022 acquisitions of Arena, GBT and Biohaven. The acquired IPR&D included **$5.0 billion from Arena**, **$3.0 billion from GBT** and **$450 million from Biohaven**.

Partly offsetting those additions was a **$200 million impairment** of an IPR&D asset acquired in the Array acquisition, for an unapproved indication of symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy linked to a lamin A/C gene mutation. Pfizer said the Phase 3 trial reached futility at a pre-planned interim analysis. (2022 Form 10-K, Notes 2 and 4, pp. 59–60, 67–68; Note 10, p. 79.)

Fiscal 2025 operating expenses as a percentage of net sales rose **36 basis points company-wide**, **44 basis points in Walmart U.S.**, and **44 basis points in Sam’s Club U.S.** The filing attributes the increases to:

- **Company-wide:** Higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan, increased marketing, and higher depreciation expenses.
- **Walmart U.S.:** Increased marketing, higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan, and increased depreciation expenses.
- **Sam’s Club U.S.:** Higher compensation-related expenses—including associate wage investments and higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan—and elevated technology spending.

Walmart International’s ratio **decreased** in fiscal 2025, so the filing does not give an explanation for an increase there. (Form 10-K, pp. 39–42)

The filing attributes fiscal 2026 gross-profit-rate increases to:

- **Company-wide:** disciplined inventory management in Walmart U.S. and growth in higher-margin businesses globally.
- **Walmart U.S.** (up 22 basis points): disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses.
- **Sam’s Club U.S.** (up 4 basis points): operational efficiencies and higher margins in fuel.

Walmart International’s rate decreased, so it is not among the segments with an increase. (Form 10-K, pp. 35, 39, 41)

The filing says Permian and Guyana growth was offset by **divestments, the expropriation of ExxonMobil’s Russian interests, and lower production entitlements resulting from higher prices**. Easing government-mandated curtailments partly counterbalanced those effects. (Form 10-K, p. 52)

Pfizer attributes the roughly **$1.1 billion favorable change** in Other (income)/deductions—net to equity-security results and lower net interest expense, partly offset by higher intangible-asset impairment charges (2023 Form 10-K, MD&A, p. 40; Note 4, p. 73).

The largest favorable driver was the swing in equity securities: Pfizer recorded **net gains of $1.590 billion in 2023**, compared with **net losses of $1.273 billion in 2022**. The 2023 gains included a **$1.7 billion realized gain on Telavant** and **$297 million of unrealized gains on Cerevel**, partly offset by **$292 million of unrealized losses on BioNTech**. The 2022 losses included **$986 million of unrealized losses** on BioNTech, Allogene and Arvinas.

**Net interest expense fell by $402 million**, from $987 million to $585 million. Interest expense rose from $1.238 billion to $2.209 billion, driven by the **$31 billion of senior unsecured notes issued in May 2023** to help finance Seagen. But interest income rose more—from $251 million to $1.624 billion—because Pfizer earned more on investing the debt proceeds, more than offsetting the higher interest expense.

A major offset was impairment: certain asset impairment charges rose from **$421 million to $3.024 billion**. Pfizer says 2023 charges included impairments of etrasimod/Velsipity IPR&D, Prevnar 13 developed technology rights, and other assets, largely reflecting changes in development plans, commercial forecasts, competition or prioritization decisions.

Other changes in Note 4 also affected the total. More royalty-related income and greater income from the Haleon/Consumer Healthcare joint venture were favorable. Less favorable changes included lower net periodic benefit credits, higher legal-matter costs, and lower collaboration and out-licensing income. The “Other, net” line was also more favorable in 2023. Together, the itemized components reconcile to the reported move from **$217 million of deductions in 2022** to **$835 million of income in 2023**.

ExxonMobil attributes the sharp 2022 rise in refining margins to **demand recovering faster than available refining supply**:

- Gasoline and diesel demand returned to pre-pandemic levels, while jet fuel demand remained below historical levels because of continuing COVID-19 effects.
- Pandemic-era refinery shutdowns and a lack of investment reduced industry capacity, tightening the market. The filing also notes that industry rationalization had taken more than 3 million barrels per day of capacity offline.
- Supply-chain constraints coincided with the continued demand recovery.

In its earnings analysis, ExxonMobil additionally points to **increased demand, low inventories, and stronger trading and marketing margins** as factors behind improved refining conditions. (Form 10-K, pp. 47, 53–54)

Growth in Card Services loans, reflecting more new accounts and higher revolving balances; higher commercial-and-industrial losses, particularly in Technology, Media & Telecommunications and Healthcare; and estimated borrower-fraud losses in certain secured lending facilities.

Pfizer attributes the increase in IPR&D’s gross carrying amount—from $18.893 billion to $21.760 billion, up about $2.9 billion—primarily to **$8.0 billion of IPR&D acquired with Metsera** in November 2025. The increase was partly offset by **$3.903 billion of IPR&D impairments** and by transfers of **$600 million for Padcev** and **$590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna)** from IPR&D to developed technology rights.

Pfizer says the 2025 intangible-asset impairments were primarily driven by **changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts**. The largest IPR&D charges were **$1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin** and **$820 million each for Tukysa (tucatinib) and osivelotor**. These figures and explanations appear in Notes 4 and 10 of Pfizer’s 2025 Form 10-K.

**Three filings identify a group acting collectively as the CODM:**

- **JPMorgan Chase** — the **Operating Committee**, whose members act collectively as the Firm’s CODM. (2024 Form 10-K, Note 32, p. 313)
- **Berkshire Hathaway** — the **Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, the Vice Chairman of Insurance Operations, and the Vice Chairman of Non-Insurance Operations**. The filing says these executives together constitute the CODM. (Note 26, p. K-108)
- **ExxonMobil** — the **Management Committee**, considered collectively, not in individual capacities. It comprises the **CEO, CFO, and two Senior Vice Presidents** who oversee the Upstream and Product Solutions businesses. (Note 18, p. 108)

The other five filings do not identify a collective CODM: **NVIDIA, Pfizer, and Boeing** name an individual CEO; **Apple and Walmart** do not identify a group acting collectively in their segment disclosures.

Only **Berkshire Hathaway** and **ExxonMobil** disclose the cumulative excess of current or replacement inventory cost over LIFO carrying value at fiscal year-end 2021:

| Company | Excess at year-end 2021 |
|---|---:|
